facts.text: The red wattlebird is the second largest species of Australian honeyeater, after the yellow wattlebird.
facts.quote: At 33–37 cm (13–14+1⁄2 in) in length, it is the second largest species of Australian honeyeater, after the yellow wattlebird.

facts.text: It has distinctive pinkish-red wattles dangling on either side of its neck.
facts.quote: The distinctive pinkish-red wattles dangle from the lower rear corner of the ear coverts on either side of the neck

facts.text: Its brush-tipped tongue has over a hundred bristles that soak up nectar by capillary action.
facts.quote: The tongue can extend well beyond the tip of the bill, and is divided at the end to form a brush-like structure with over a hundred bristles that soak up nectar by capillary action.

facts.text: Pairs of red wattlebirds appear to duet, the male giving a loud cackle and the female a whistling call.
facts.quote: Pairs of birds appear to duet, particularly at food sources, with the male producing a loud cackle and the female a whistling call.

facts.text: It is one of the largest nectar-feeding birds in the world.
facts.quote: With an average weight of 100–120 grams (3.5–4.2 oz), the red wattlebird is one of the largest nectar-feeding birds in the world

facts.text: It prefers flowers with easy access to nectar and favours eucalypts, banksias, grasstrees and emu bushes.
facts.quote: The red wattlebird prioritises visiting flowers that produce a lot of nectar, such as those of eucalypts, banksias, grasstrees (Xanthorrhoea), and emu bushes (Eremophila). It often prefers plants with easy access to nectar, rather than those with tubular flowers

facts.text: Over winter it gathers in larger groups of up to several hundred birds.
facts.quote: A loud and active bird, the red wattlebird is found in pairs, in a small family group, or alone during the breeding season, and gathers in larger groups of up to several hundred birds over winter.

facts.text: It builds a cup-shaped nest of sticks and leaves in a tree fork, usually a eucalypt, and raises one or two broods a year.
facts.quote: The nest is a cup-shaped structure formed from sticks and leaves, lined with bark, grass, and hair, between 2 and 16 metres (7 and 50 ft) above ground, usually in the forked branches of a tree—generally a eucalypt.
